ch08.title: The Twelve and the Women
ch08.b002: In the spring of A.D. 28 the thirteen set out early on the morning of Tuesday, March 30, taking the road down the Jordan valley, and on the afternoon of Friday, April 2, they came to Bethany. Passing through Jericho they stopped to rest, and while the others sat in the shade, Judas Iscariot went off to the bank of an old friend of his family and deposited part of the common funds there. It was the first time the apostolic purse had ever held more than it needed. Judas folded the receipt and tucked it inside his robe with a look of quiet satisfaction. The money would lie in Jericho, untouched, for a long time to come. It would stay there until the day they passed through Jericho once more, and none of them could have guessed, that spring, what kind of journey that would be.
ch08.b003: For nearly three weeks in Jerusalem the Master forbade the apostles to do any public preaching. They were to teach privately and to work with people one by one. From near and far came men and women seeking healing for their bodies and comfort for troubled minds, and the pressure was so great that Jesus had little rest; tents were pitched at Gethsemane, and he went back and forth between Bethany and the garden to escape the crowds. For John Zebedee those three weeks were hard to bear. He was still the youngest of the twelve, and he had a young man’s impatience. In Galilee hundreds had followed the Master. Yet here, in the great city itself, the city of the temple and the high priest, they were made to go about with lowered voices.
ch08.b004: On the afternoon of their second Sabbath in Jerusalem, as the whole company was setting out for the temple services, John caught at the Master’s sleeve. There was something he wanted to show him, he said; would he come? He led Jesus out through one of the city gates to the pool called Bethesda. Under the five porches that surrounded it the sick lay packed together. Every so often the reddish, warm water of the spring bubbled up from below, and the people believed that whoever first entered the pool after the water stirred would be healed. The air smelled of sulphur and of wounds that would not close. John wanted the Master to see it all. Surely he could not look upon this and do nothing. One single display of power here, and all Jerusalem would be astounded and would come to believe in the kingdom.
ch08.b005: “Master,” John said, “⟦Q 147:3.2⟧is there nothing we can do for them?⟦/Q⟧”
ch08.b006: Jesus looked at him. Then he asked why John would tempt him to turn aside from the path he had chosen. Why did John keep wanting wonders and cures in the place of the proclamation of eternal truth? And yet he called him “my son.” He could not do what John wished, he said; but John should gather the sick and afflicted together, and he would speak to them words of good cheer and comfort.
ch08.b007: John’s face burned. It had been a rebuke. But there had not been one drop of anger in it. He went along the porches calling the people together. Jesus told them that some of them were ill because of years of wrong living, some through the accidents of time, some because of the mistakes of their forebears. But all of them were God’s children; however heavily the bonds of time might press on them, the God of eternity loved them. To be healed of a bodily ailment would be a marvel, he said, but to be cleansed of the sickness of the spirit was a greater thing still. Many believed. And one man, who had lain there for years, crushed by discouragement and the weakness of a troubled mind, always waiting for someone to lower him into the water, rolled up his bed and carried it home, though it was the Sabbath. Helping himself, it turned out, was the one thing he had needed to do.
ch08.b008: Then the Master told John they had better leave before the chief priests and scribes arrived and took offense. The two of them went back to the temple and slipped in among their companions. John never told the other apostles about that afternoon. He did not tell even his brother James. At first it was shame that kept him silent: it was he who had tried to put the Master to the test. But as the days passed the silence became something else. He wanted to keep that afternoon for himself—the voice that rebuked him and called him son in the same breath, the way the Master had set aside John’s eager plan and sat down instead among the sick. It was the first day on which the youngest apostle’s hidden pride began to make room for something other than itself.
ch08.b010: That same Sabbath evening a fire was burning in Lazarus’s garden at Bethany. Nathaniel brought out a question he had been carrying around all afternoon. The rule that one should do to others as one would wish them to do to oneself was a fine rule, he said, but what of the lustful man, who might turn those very words to his own ends? Being the group’s philosopher, he even supplied an example. Before he had quite finished, the Master was on his feet. He pointed straight at him and spoke his name twice. What kind of thinking was going on in his heart? Did he not receive the teaching as one born of the spirit? When he had spoken that rule, Jesus said, he had been speaking to men of high ideals, not to those who would twist it into a license for evil.
ch08.b011: The fireside went still. Nathaniel rose, red to the ears. The Master must not think, he said, that he approved such a reading; he had asked only because he feared many would misunderstand, and he had hoped to learn more. Jesus answered that he knew Nathaniel well and knew no such idea had a home in his mind. What disappointed him was how often they all failed to give a truly spiritual meaning to his plain teachings, which he had to put in human words, as men must speak. Then he unfolded that single rule into six levels: the level of the flesh, the level of the feelings, the level of mind, the level of brotherly love, the moral level, and last and highest, the spiritual level. At the top, he said, the rule became a command to treat every man as you conceive God would treat him. Do to others, he told them, what you know I would do in your place.
ch08.b012: Long after the Master had gone in, the apostles sat on, turning his words over. Nothing he had said to them before had astonished them more. The others were grateful that Nathaniel had had the nerve to ask such a question. But Nathaniel himself, lying awake that night, could not shake off the moment when that finger had pointed at him. He was an honest man, and nothing stings an honest man like being misunderstood. It was some days before he could make a joke of it. When a philosopher chooses an illustration, he said, he would do well to pick a less vivid one. Philip laughed, and then at last Nathaniel laughed a little too.
ch08.b013: In those same days Simon, an influential Pharisee of Jerusalem and a halfhearted believer, invited the Master, with Peter, James, and John, to a meal at his house. John remembered that evening for a long time. When the wealthy gave a banquet it was the custom to leave the doors open, so that beggars from the street could stand along the walls behind the couches and catch the scraps tossed to them. Among the beggars that night was a woman with her hair let down. She had once kept one of the well-known houses near the temple’s court of the gentiles, but she had believed the good news of the kingdom and given that life up. She came and stood behind Jesus where he reclined at the table, poured the contents of a large flask of perfumed lotion over his feet, wet them with her tears, and wiped them with her hair. The heavy fragrance filled the room. John saw Simon’s face harden.
ch08.b014: The Master told Simon about a moneylender with two debtors, one owing five hundred denarii and one owing fifty. If both debts were forgiven, which man would love him more? Then he pointed to the woman. She had done for him, he said, everything that Simon as host had neglected to do; one who has been forgiven much loves much. He took the woman by the hand and raised her up, and told her that her sins were forgiven, that she should not be cast down by the unkindness of others, and that she should go on in the joy and liberty of the kingdom. John watched that hand lift her—the hand of a woman whom respectable people crossed the street to avoid. Something in him, the hot thing that was quite capable of wanting fire called down from heaven, grew a little quieter that night.
ch08.b015: As they were leaving, the Master turned to his host. He knew, he told Simon, how he was torn between faith and doubt, how fear and pride held him; and he prayed that Simon might know a change as great as the one already worked in the heart of his uninvited and unwelcome guest. That night, back in the camp at Gethsemane, Jesus talked long with all of them. What mattered, he said, was not how fast a man went but in which direction. What you are becoming day by day matters far more than where you stand today. That woman seemed to stand far below Simon, but she was moving toward God, and Simon was standing still on his height. John sat in the shadow of the lamp, listening, and took the measure of his own place. One of the three who stayed nearest the Master. He had always thought of that as a high place. Tonight the words were telling him that place was nothing and direction was everything.
ch08.b017: In the last week of April they started back toward Galilee. At Jericho six men attached themselves to the party, which numbered about thirty. They said they wished to become disciples; in truth they were spies sent by the Sanhedrin. Thomas Didymus, whose task was managing the itinerary, studied each new face. One man had come with no baggage at all; another never asked a question but kept his ears open. Thomas did not like them. But if he voiced suspicion without proof, Peter would only call him mean and suspicious again. So he held his tongue and did his sums.
ch08.b018: Peter preached at the crossing of the Jordan, and near Amathus so many people gathered that they stayed three days. They could not leave until early on the Sabbath morning, the first day of May. The spies’ eyes glittered: setting out on a journey on the Sabbath! But just before they left, the Master called Andrew and told him, in the hearing of everyone, to go only a thousand yards that day, the distance the law allowed. Thomas smiled to himself. In all his time arranging their travels, he had never planned so short a day.
ch08.b019: Yet even that short road brought trouble. Ripening wheat stood close on both sides of the narrow way, and some of the apostles, being hungry, plucked heads of grain and rubbed them in their hands to eat. The spies came up to Andrew and told him that rubbing grain on the Sabbath broke the law. Andrew answered that if chewing was allowed, rubbing could hardly be much more work; why quibble over such trifles? Stung at being called quibblers, they hurried to Jesus, who was walking with Matthew, and complained. The Master reminded them how David, when he was hungry, had eaten the showbread in the house of God. The Sabbath was made for man, he said, not man for the Sabbath. And if they were there to watch his words, he would tell them plainly that the Son of Man was lord even of the Sabbath. For the rest of the day the spies walked by themselves. Thomas looked at Andrew’s back. Here was a man who could not bring himself to praise anyone, and today he had won an argument. Thomas found that oddly satisfying.
ch08.b020: The Tent City by the Sea
ch08.b021: Around noon on Monday, May 3, they came by boat from Tarichea to Bethsaida. From that day until October 3, five whole months, a tented city stood on the shore in front of Zebedee’s house. Seekers after truth, people hoping to be healed, and people who had simply come to look rose and fell in number between five hundred and fifteen hundred. David Zebedee had charge of it all, and the Alpheus twins helped him. The twins loved the work: lining up the tents, setting the order at the well, finding a place for a family that had come in late. They might grasp only half of the mysteries of the kingdom, but they could drive a tent peg straight. A short way to the south, Elman, a Syrian physician, set up a tented infirmary for the sick with a corps of twenty-five young women and twelve men. The Master went there no fewer than three times a week and touched each sufferer with his own hand.
ch08.b022: Peter was in charge of the school of evangelists, and every morning the apostles taught the young men. At least one day a week the apostles went out fishing and sold the catch to David, and one week in each month they were free to go home to their families. That summer the Master went off alone into the hills more often than at any other time. Whenever he did, he took with him any two apostles who happened to be free. Thomas went several times. He would sit in the shade of a rock and watch the Master for hours. Jesus’s face changed again and again, as if light were passing over it. It seemed that he was speaking, but no sound reached them. Thomas tried to measure it. What was that face looking at? With whom was it speaking? But once again there was nothing he could measure. He knew only that each time the Master came down, his face was a little more tranquil than before.
ch08.b023: Two evenings a week the Master would sit in a sheltered corner of Zebedee’s garden and talk privately with anyone who wished it. One evening Thomas asked what he had long been wanting to ask. Why must a man be born of the spirit? Was rebirth needed to escape the evil one? And what, after all, was evil? The Master separated for him evil, sin, and iniquity: to transgress the Father’s will without knowing it; to transgress it knowingly; and to go on transgressing it, knowingly and stubbornly, to the end. Man is born imperfect, he said, but imperfection is not sin. Man has not fallen from some perfect height; he is climbing up from below toward God. Thomas had been confused, Jesus told him, by the doctrines of the Greeks and the errors of the Persians.
ch08.b024: Thomas held on to those words for a long time. Not a beginning in ruin, but a beginning in ascent. Ever since he lost his twin sister when he was nine years old, he had looked on the world as a place that was always falling down. And this man looked at the same world and saw a stairway. That night Thomas understood a great deal. Then the Master asked him not to speak of these things to the others until he had returned to the Father. Thomas kept that promise. It was the first secret he had ever been given.
ch08.b025: On the second Sabbath before the second tour, in the synagogue at Capernaum, Thomas saw something more. When the sermon was over the sick crowded around the Master, and the leader of the spies pushed forward a man with a withered hand, having put him up to asking whether it was lawful to be healed on the Sabbath. Jesus saw at once that the man had been sent. If a sheep fell into a pit on the Sabbath, he asked them, would they not lift it out? And how much more was a man worth than a sheep! In the silence that followed he had the man stand beside him and told him to stretch out his hand. The man opened it. Thomas held his breath and watched the fingers straighten one by one. The hand was calloused. It was a hand that had worked stone. The man was a stone mason. Thomas had once been a stone mason too. He knew what it meant to be a mason who could not grip a hammer. When the people were minded to turn on the Pharisees, the Master calmed them: he had told them it was lawful to do good on the Sabbath, not to do harm. The furious Pharisees hurried off to Herod at Tiberias, Sabbath or no Sabbath, but Herod waved them away and told them to take their complaint to Jerusalem. The mason, Aaron, went back to dressing stone. For the rest of his life, whenever Thomas heard a chisel ring on rock, he remembered that Sabbath.
ch08.b027: On another evening, in the same corner of the garden, Nathaniel asked a different question. He was beginning to understand, he said, why the Master would not heal everyone indiscriminately. But he still could not understand why a loving Father allowed so many of his children on earth to suffer so much. The Father does not purposely afflict his children, Jesus told him. Suffering comes from the imperfections of a world still in time, from the consequences of sin, from the harvest of persistent rebellion; it is not a punishment God hands down at whim on the wrongdoer. It was an old habit, he said, to blame God for everything man did not understand.
ch08.b028: That same evening John also asked. Why did people who seemed innocent suffer so? The porches of Bethesda were still before his eyes. The Master told him the story of Job: how his three friends, each with plausible words, only made his pain worse; how Job, finding no answer among men, turned to God; how at last he cried out that his Vindicator lived. The Father, Jesus said, does not speak out of the whirlwind but within the human heart, as a still, small voice. Did John not understand that God lived within him, that God had become what John was so that he might make John what God is?
ch08.b029: John turned the words over for many days. That conversation in the garden changed the whole of his later life. Yet he too kept it to himself until after the Master was gone. That summer three men sat before the Master in the same garden, each with his own question, and each of them held his answer alone for years. When Nathaniel learned of it much later, he laughed. We were all drawing water from the same well, he said, and each of us was peering into his own bucket.
ch08.b030: Toward the end of the summer a self-styled prophet named Kirmeth arrived from Bagdad, fell into trances, and raved about strange visions. The camp was in an uproar. Simon Zelotes wanted the man dealt with roughly, but the Master let him have his way for a few days. Those who listened soon saw that what he taught was nonsense. Before the Master stepped in on his behalf, however, David Zebedee and a self-appointed committee took Kirmeth out into the lake, plunged him under several times, and advised him to go and found a camp of his own. Whenever Nathaniel told the story, he put on a solemn face. It was not a baptism, he would say, merely a rather thorough piece of counsel.
ch08.b031: About that time in Jerusalem, Abraham, a young and influential member of the Sanhedrin, openly embraced the Master’s teachings and was baptized by Abner in the pool of Siloam. All Jerusalem was agog. Abraham gave all his worldly goods to the apostolic treasury, and that gift made it possible to send out the hundred newly trained evangelists at once. As Judas Iscariot copied the sum into his accounts, his pen hung still for a long moment. A member of the Sanhedrin had come over to their side. To Judas this meant more than a figure in a ledger: the upper ranks were beginning to move. That evening he sat down to supper with a brighter face than anyone else at the table.
ch08.b032: On Friday afternoon, October 1, the final meeting was held in the large, enlarged front room of Zebedee’s house. Six Pharisees from Jerusalem sat in the front row, and the crowd filled the house and pressed all around it. Then there came a sound from above of tiles being lifted. A shaft of sunlight fell into the room, and a small couch, hanging from ropes, came slowly down. On it lay a paralytic from Capernaum, a man who had talked with the newly healed mason. Unable to get in by either the front door or the back, he had had his friends fetch ladders. He did not wish to disturb the teaching, he said; he wanted to be made whole so that he might serve in the kingdom. The Master told him not to be afraid; his sins were forgiven. The Pharisees’ faces went rigid. Knowing what they were thinking, Jesus asked what difference there was between saying your sins are forgiven and saying arise and walk. Then he told the sick man to take up his bed and go home. And the man walked out in front of them all. Nathaniel looked up at the hole in the ceiling. Old Zebedee, he was sure, was already reckoning the cost of the roof. But that day, for once, he kept the joke to himself. Just then messengers from the Sanhedrin arrived to call the spies home. Of the six, three went back, and three were baptized by Peter in the lake that same day.
ch08.b034: On the second preaching tour of Galilee, which began in October and lasted three months, only James and John went with the Master. The other apostles scattered, each with about a dozen young evangelists. John followed Jesus as he covered two towns in a single day. The Master deliberately worked no wonders. And yet people began to be healed. Once, when a sick child touched him, John heard him stop and say that he perceived life had gone out from him. Every time someone was healed, the Master charged him to tell no one; every one of them went home and told everyone. Between that charge and that rumor John began, for the first time, to sense how lonely the Master was.
ch08.b035: The Master visited the scattered groups in turn. One evening, with the group under Simon Zelotes, Simon asked him why some people were so much happier than others; was contentment a matter of religious experience? Much depended, Jesus said, on a man’s willingness to be led by the Father’s spirit within him. And much of man’s sorrow came from disappointed ambition and wounded pride. When a man had done his honest best, he should cheerfully accept his lot. As he listened, John watched Simon’s face. Here was a man who had given up a high place among the Zealots. Simon nodded, but there was something heavy in the nod. At Gamala, Philip asked how it was that the Scriptures told them to fear the Lord, while the Master would have them look to the Father without fear. In the beginning, Jesus answered, men could learn reverence only through fear; but he had come to lead them on from reverence to love. Philip counted the answer off on his fingers to remember it. Fear, reverence, love. Three things; easy to keep count of.
ch08.b036: On Thursday, December 30, a rainy day, all the groups came back to Bethsaida. For two or three days Zebedee’s house rang with the young evangelists telling what had happened to them, and even the older apostles learned from listening. Of the hundred and seventeen, only about seventy-five had come through the test.
ch08.b037: On Sunday evening, January 16, A.D. 29, at Bethsaida, the Master spoke briefly. Tomorrow, he said, we will set apart ten women for the ministering work of the kingdom. The room froze. In their world a man was not supposed to greet even his own wife in a public place. In the synagogue women were kept to the gallery. There were rabbis who taught that it was better to burn the words of the law than to deliver them to women. The apostles had heard many times that in the kingdom there was neither male nor female. They had not imagined it meant this.
ch08.b038: Nathaniel listened to the names and called up each face as it came. Looking after the apostles’ families was his task, and he knew those households well. Susanna, daughter of the former chazan of the Nazareth synagogue. Joanna, wife of Chuza, the steward of Herod Antipas. Elizabeth, daughter of a wealthy Jew of Tiberias and Sepphoris. Nasanta, Elman’s daughter. Celta, daughter of a Roman centurion. Agaman, a widow of Damascus. Then Martha, the elder sister of Andrew and Peter; Nathaniel saw Peter’s eyes go wide. Milcha, Thomas’s cousin; Thomas began to say something and stopped. Rachel, sister-in-law of Jude, the Master’s brother. And Ruth, Matthew’s eldest daughter. Matthew bowed his head. Nathaniel saw what was stirring beneath that bowed head. A publican’s daughter was being set apart as a teacher of the kingdom.
ch08.b039: The Master let the women organize themselves and told Judas Iscariot to provide money for their equipment and their pack animals. The women chose Susanna as their chief and Joanna as their treasurer. From then on they managed their own funds and never again drew on Judas. Judas entered the expense in his ledger and ruled a line beneath it, a straight line. But that evening Nathaniel noticed Judas watching Joanna’s hands as she counted, watching them for a long while. Whether it was admiration or something else, Nathaniel could not tell.
ch08.b040: When the third tour began, the women traveled at the rear of the company, and at meetings they sat together in front of the speaker, to his right. At Magdala they showed for the first time why they were needed. Andrew had laid down strict rules for the apostles about personal work with women, especially women of doubtful character. But the women evangelists could freely go into houses where no apostle could set foot. In one such house Martha and Rachel told a woman that the doors of the kingdom were open even to one like her. Her name was Mary. The next day Peter baptized her. Nathaniel saw Peter’s face as he came back from the water: the face of a younger brother who had just baptized someone his older sister had brought in. None of the twelve knew then that on the last day, when almost all the apostles would scatter and flee, these women would be there, every one of them.
ch08.b041: At the Master’s direction Andrew also handed over the Sabbath services of the apostolic party to the women. Since women could not lead worship in the synagogue, they put Joanna in charge and borrowed the banquet hall of Herod’s new palace, Herod being away at Julias in Perea. Joanna read the passages of Scripture about the work of women in the religious life of Israel and spoke of Miriam, Deborah, and Esther. Nathaniel stood at the very back and listened. He saw Martha sitting with her head high, as if she had been doing this all her life. Late that evening Andrew asked the Master whether there was any truth in the belief that the bright new star lately seen in the sky foretold the birth of a great man. The Master began by saying that the courses of the stars had nothing whatever to do with human events, and went on to dismantle every superstition in turn: the entrails of slaughtered animals, charms and relics, the casting of lots, the reading of dreams. Listening to the list, Nathaniel thought of the old women of his home town of Cana. If they had heard this, they would have fainted dead away.
ch08.b043: Not long after Magdala, the Master stayed behind with the younger teachers and the women and sent the twelve out ahead in pairs: Andrew and Peter, James and John, Philip and Nathaniel, Thomas and Matthew, the twins, and Simon Zelotes with Judas Iscariot. They were not to go into any city of the gentiles or into Samaria, he told them, but to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Two sparrows might be sold for a penny, yet God forgot not one of them; even the hairs of their heads were numbered, so they need not fear. And they were to meet him at Nazareth on Friday, March 4.
ch08.b044: When the pairs were named, Thomas’s ear caught on the last one. Simon Zelotes and Judas Iscariot. The fiery Zealot and the calculating Judean. One thought in terms of the sword, the other in terms of the ledger, and now they were to walk the same road. Watching their backs as they set off side by side, Thomas wondered what they would talk about on the way. Probably, he thought, they would both talk about when the kingdom would show its true face—each of them picturing a different one.
ch08.b045: Thomas walked with Matthew. For the first few days neither of them said much. Thomas counted miles and Matthew counted money. Then one evening, at the well of a strange village, Matthew suddenly began to talk about Ruth. What had he said when his daughter told him she would take up this work? Nothing, he said. He had not been able to say a word. He had only nodded. Thomas just listened. Then he talked about Milcha—his cousin, who as a little girl had always tagged along behind him. Sometimes when he looked at her, he said, he thought of another sister. It was the nearest Thomas ever came to telling anyone that story. Matthew did not ask. That night they slept under the same eaves.
ch08.b046: At Nazareth, on the day of their arrival, the Master sent Thomas to the ruler of the synagogue to arrange for him to speak at the Sabbath morning service. Thomas handled it neatly. But as he left the synagogue, the looks of the townspeople troubled him. They were not glad looks. A local man had made a great name for himself and come home, and there was jealousy and resentment in their eyes. He heard them muttering that Jesus had never once come back, that he had not even visited his brother and sisters. That afternoon Andrew and Peter, the last to arrive, reached the camp on the highlands north of the town. The Master walked through Nazareth alone. No one recognized him. He passed the house of his childhood and the carpenter shop, sat for half an hour on the hill, and came down as the trumpet sounded the setting of the sun. Thomas watched his back from far off. And he could not bring himself to measure what he had seen in that face.
ch08.b048: The Sabbath dawned fine. All Nazareth came to the synagogue, and there was not room enough; many of the apostolic company had to stand outside. The ruler of the synagogue handed Jesus the roll. It was the very manuscript he himself had presented to that synagogue as a young man, but no one present seemed to remember. The Master read from Deuteronomy, the passage that says the commandment is not far off in heaven or across the sea but near, in one’s mouth and in one’s heart. Then he turned to Isaiah, to the words about the spirit of the Lord resting on one sent with good tidings for the poor and release for the captives. He rolled up the scroll, handed it back, sat down, and said that today these words were fulfilled. For almost fifteen minutes he spoke about the sons and daughters of God. Many marveled at his gracious words.
ch08.b049: When the service ended and the Master stepped down among those who wanted to ask questions, the air changed. Hired roughs were circling the fringe of the crowd. The disciples who had been outside pushed their way in and tried to lead him out, but he would not go. People jostled him and pointed their fingers. Your brother is a common workman, they said, your sisters live here, we know your mother; so why do no wonders here? Half in jest the Master answered that yes, he was Joseph’s son, the carpenter, and he was not surprised to hear the proverb about the physician healing himself. A prophet, he said, is not without honor except in his own country. But he loved the people of the town where he had grown up.
ch08.b050: Left to himself, he would have quieted the crowd gently. But Simon Zelotes could not hold back. With Nahor, one of the younger evangelists, he gathered the Master’s friends out of the crowd into a body and ordered the Master’s enemies to clear out. The other apostles let their own anger loose. They had heard a hundred times that a soft answer turns away wrath. But to see their beloved teacher mocked hurt more than the teaching could hold. Their anger was oil on the fire. The roughs seized the Master and hustled him out of the synagogue. The crowd surged out after them, and Thomas, swept along by it, fought to keep the Master’s back in sight. They made for a steep hill close by. Gravel skittered away under their feet. It was the brow of a cliff.
ch08.b051: One sentence went round and round in Thomas’s head. I went to the synagogue. I arranged this Sabbath sermon. He could not breathe. Then the Master turned. Slowly, toward the hands that held him. And he folded his arms. He said nothing. He simply faced them. Thomas could hear the wind. Someone’s grip slid from the Master’s robe and fell away. The Master took a step forward. The crowd parted. Another step. A way opened. No one stopped him. He walked out between them.
ch08.b052: Thomas stood where he was and watched the crowd close up again behind him. He could not explain it. There had been no lightning of power, no heavenly host. There had been one man with his arms folded, and hundreds of people who stood aside of their own accord. He could not prove it. But he had seen it. And that day, for the first time, he knew in his body what might lie at the end of the road he was walking with this man. Today the crowd had stood aside. One day there would come a crowd that would not. Thomas wiped his shaking hands on his robe. Then he started walking toward the Master’s back. What else could he do? He had to go.
ch08.b054: When they reached the camp, the Master told the disciples all that had happened and had them make ready to leave for Capernaum early the next morning. Simon Zelotes sat all evening with his back to the fire. He believed he had done right. At the same time he knew what he had spoiled. No one blamed him, and that was harder to bear than blame. Nathaniel came and sat down beside him, but he made no jokes. For a long while the two of them looked into the fire without speaking.
ch08.b055: On Sunday morning they left Nazareth by different roads, and by noon on Thursday, March 10, they had all reassembled at Bethsaida. So the third tour came to its rough end. They did not return as a triumphant band of crusaders who had conquered everything before them. They came back as preachers with a dream broken, and for that very reason sober and serious. That spring, little by little, they were beginning to learn that the kingdom would come only through much sorrow and bitter disappointment. Behind them the women quietly unpacked. Not one of them had turned back.
ch08.b057: The events follow Papers 147–150: the journey to Jerusalem, the deposit at Jericho, and the ban on public preaching (147:2.1–2.2); the pool of Bethesda (147:3.1–3.6); Nathaniel’s question in Lazarus’s garden (147:4.1–4.10); the meal at Simon’s house and the talk that evening (147:5.1–5.8); the six spies who joined at Jericho, the thousand-yard Sabbath journey, and the grainfield (147:6.1–6.5); the tented city at Bethsaida, Elman’s infirmary, and the two apostles taken into the hills (148:0.1–3.5); the garden talks with Thomas, Nathaniel, and John (148:4.1–6.12); the healing of the stone mason’s withered hand on the Sabbath (148:7.1–7.4); Kirmeth, and Abraham’s conversion and gift (148:8.1–8.5); the paralytic let down through the roof and the baptism of three spies (148:9.1–9.4); the second tour, its companions, and the unconscious healings (149:0.3, 149:1.1–1.3); the questions of Simon Zelotes and Philip (149:5.1–5.4, 149:6.1–6.3); the return (149:7.1–7.3); the setting apart of the ten women and Judas’s funds for their equipment (150:1.1–1.3); Magdala and Mary Magdalene (150:2.1–2.3); the women’s Sabbath service and the talk on superstition (150:3.1–3.12); the pairs of apostles and their sending (150:4.1–4.4); and the visit to Nazareth, the synagogue, Simon Zelotes’s blunder, and the cliff (150:6.3–9.5).
ch08.b058: Character details are drawn from Paper 139: John’s hidden pride and his wish to call down fire (139:4.4–4.8); Nathaniel’s honesty, humor, and care of the families (139:6.3–6.7); Thomas’s charge of the itinerary, his former trade as a stone mason, the loss of his twin sister, and Peter’s early complaint against him (139:8.2–8.10); the twins’ management of the crowds (139:9.3); Simon Zelotes’s Zealot temper (139:11.1–11.4); and Matthew’s past as a publican (139:7.1–7.3).
ch08.b059: Added fiction includes the inner thoughts and feelings of the characters (John’s shame and the meaning of his silence, the sting Nathaniel felt at being misunderstood, Thomas’s guilt at having arranged the synagogue sermon); sensory detail at the pool, the banquet room, and the cliff; Nathaniel’s jokes; the talk between Thomas and Matthew about a daughter and a cousin; Judas’s thoughts as he recorded Abraham’s gift and his watching Joanna’s hands; Philip counting on his fingers; the twins’ pleasure in camp work; and Simon and Nathaniel by the fire after Nazareth. That Judas’s deposit remained at Jericho until the last journey to Jerusalem is in the text; its weight is placed here to look ahead to later chapters.
ch08.b060: The words of Jesus are retold, not quoted, following the sense of the text.
